---
title: Best Time to See the Northern Lights
h1: Best Time to See the Northern Lights
---

[Check tonight’s local reading →](/)

There is no single best clock time for the whole United States. The best time to see northern lights depends on season, latitude, and tonight’s weather. Use this page for the year and the night in general. Use a local page for tonight’s window.

## Best time to see northern lights in a year

In Alaska and other high-latitude places, the useful season is roughly **late August through mid-April**. Midsummer nights are often too bright, even when the oval is active. June in Fairbanks is usually a darkness no. That is why Interior season is not “any month you can get a cheap ticket.”

In the Lower 48, storms can arrive in any month. Longer nights from **September through March** help. A strong storm in May still needs a dark enough sky. Equinox weeks get folklore about extra activity; we still score tonight from data, not from the calendar.

Alaska’s “when to come” belongs on the [Alaska](/forecast/alaska) page, not on a separate places URL. Fairbanks has its own tonight tool. Do not merge those two searches.

## Best time to see northern lights in a night

Aurora is a night-sky event. On this site, a slot does not count until the sun is **12 degrees below the horizon**. That is later than civil twilight, and in summer it can be much later than “after sunset.”

There is **no nationwide showtime**. “What time tonight?” is answered on each local page as a window, not as one US clock. Mid-latitude looks are often late evening. Do not wait for a fake 73% minute. On a given date the usable slot is the first dark, clear-enough hour while the oval still reaches you — which may be 9 PM in one county and 1 AM in another.

If the local card says the window is empty, standing outside at a famous clock time does not create darkness or punch a hole in the clouds.

## It depends on where you are

- **Alaska Interior / Fairbanks:** darkness and a frequent oval. Season matters as much as tonight. Solstice weeks are a darkness no.
- **Northern Minnesota, Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, Maine:** the oval is closer. Quiet nights can still be no; storm nights can be yes.
- **Colorado, Ohio, Illinois, and similar mid-latitude states:** event nights only. Most nights are no. A GO here is unusual and local.
- **Seattle and other maritime west-side cities:** winter is darker but cloudier. A clear slot after a frontal passage can matter more than Kp.

Examples: [Minnesota](/forecast/minnesota), [Maine](/forecast/maine), [Colorado](/forecast/colorado), [Alaska](/forecast/alaska), [Seattle](/forecast/seattle).

## What “best time” is not

Usable hours are not a single Instagram clock, not “midnight everywhere,” and not the minute a friend in another state posted a photo. Magnetic latitude, skyglow, and the cloud deck at your headline point decide whether that photo is relevant.

We also do not treat moon phase as a nationwide kill switch. A bright moon on a horizon-only oval can block GO. An overhead storm can still be worth a look. That call is local.

## How to use this page with tonight’s table

This guide is the seasonal and nightly framing. The ranked list is [Where to see the northern lights](/guides/where-to-see-northern-lights). Standing advice is [How to see the northern lights](/guides/how-to-see-northern-lights). Gate order is [How we decide](/methodology).

If you booked travel, read the Alaska or Fairbanks page for season, then use those URLs for the actual night. If you are in an event-only state, the usable window might be “the next strong storm with a dark north horizon,” which could be this week or not this year.

A photographer who can wait all night still uses the local window, not a blog’s 10 PM Eastern default. Stay for 30–60 minutes if that window is open. Leave if the card is NO for oval reach; no clock will fix that.

Related: [Tonight home](/) · [Near me](/near-me)

## Equinox folklore versus data

September and March get more “the lights are coming” posts. Geomagnetic seasons have a real pattern, but a usable night is still a dark, clear, in-reach slot — not the calendar caption. A cloudy equinox is a no. A clear January night under the oval can be a yes. We will not print an equinox percent.

If you can only take one week of leave, Interior Alaska in September or March is the usual travel compromise: dark enough, less brutal than December, still not a guarantee. That is a season choice. Tonight remains a separate card.

## Clock time people ask for

“Is 10 PM the magic hour?” Not as a US rule. East Coast event nights often run late. Alaska winter can start earlier because darkness arrives earlier. Summer Lower 48 storms still wait for −12°. The local hours table is the clock. This guide will not invent a nationwide 10:40.

Moonrise can matter on a faint horizon oval. It does not cancel an overhead storm by itself. The live card will name moon when it blocks GO.

## Putting it together

1. Pick the place (state, city, or ZIP).
2. Read tonight’s status.
3. If you are planning a trip months out, use season on this page and on Alaska / Fairbanks.
4. If you are going out tonight, ignore season and use the window.

The best time to see northern lights is the overlap of darkness, reach, and holes in the clouds at that place. Everything else is commentary.

## Travel planning without a fake calendar

If you can only pick one week:

- **Interior Alaska:** late August–September or February–March. Dark enough, less brutal than deep winter, still weather-limited.
- **Minnesota / UP / Maine:** longer nights help. Clouds and snow squalls still veto nights.
- **Colorado / Ohio / Illinois:** do not book a week “for aurora.” Book if you already have another reason to be there, then use the tonight card.
- **Seattle:** winter is darker and cloudier. A clear slot after a front matters.

We do not sell flights. We do not guarantee a curtain in any of those windows. Season is a filter; the local page is the night.

## Darkness rule of thumb

Civil twilight is not enough. Nautical twilight is closer. This site uses sun at or below −12°. In June at high latitude that may never happen. In December it happens early. If you remember only one number from this page, remember −12°, not 10 PM.

Moon: name it when it blocks GO. Do not cancel a trip for a full moon if the oval is overhead and the sky is clear. Do cancel if the card already said horizon-only plus bright moon.

---
title: How to See the Northern Lights
h1: How to See the Northern Lights
---

[Check tonight’s local reading →](/)

This is not a solar-storm explainer. It is how to see northern lights with a dark north sky, and how to read this site’s GO / MAYBE / NO. Open a local page first. This guide does not replace a tonight card.

## How to see northern lights from the Lower 48

From the Lower 48, aurora often sits on the **northern horizon**, not overhead. A south-facing slope, a downtown skyline, or a mountain wall to the north can hide it. Leave the city if the local page says to. We do not list unverified parking lots.

If the card says horizon-only, look north along a flat, dark edge. If it says city glow, a park inside the light dome is usually still a no. Standing in Colorado or Ohio is not the same as standing under the oval in Fairbanks.

## You need real darkness

Streetlight and twilight both wash out a weak oval. On this site, slots with the sun higher than **−12°** are marked not dark yet and do not count toward GO. A phone screen in your eyes is almost as bad as a porch light. Give your eyes time.

Civil twilight is not dark enough for a faint display. “After sunset” is not the rule. If the hours table still says not dark yet, waiting on the porch does not change the sun angle.

## Wait 30–60 minutes

Aurora is not a scheduled firework. If the window is open, stay for **half an hour to an hour**. Short spikes get missed by people who step out for five minutes and leave. Patience is the part the viral clip skipped.

If the status is NO because the oval does not reach you, waiting longer does not pull the oval south. If the status is NO because of clouds, waiting only helps if the deck is actually moving — the local main issue will say so.

## A phone may show color first

Cameras collect light longer than your eyes. A green smear on a phone is not a guarantee you will see a curtain. It is a hint to keep looking. Do not treat a photo as a probability, and do not treat a photo from another state as your forecast.

A long-exposure shot from another county is not part of this product. We do not score camera settings. We score whether tonight is worth trying with your eyes in a dark north sky.

## How to read GO / MAYBE / NO

- **GO** — conditions line up well enough to try.
- **MAYBE** — possible, with a named obstacle (clouds, horizon-only, city glow).
- **NO** — not worth a special trip tonight. The oval may be out of reach, or the sky socked in.
- **UNKNOWN** — we are not guessing. Data is missing or stale.

We do not print a percent chance. A national Kp number is not a local yes. Open your city or state page for the window and the main issue. Start with that card, then this posture: face north, get dark, wait.

## What not to do

Do not drive south expecting a better oval. Do not sit on a south-facing mountain wall. Do not use high beams as a viewing aid. Do not crowd an unnamed pullout we never listed. Most of this is subtraction: remove lights, remove the wrong horizon, remove the five-minute glance.

If you still need a place, use [near me](/near-me). If you still need season, use [best time](/guides/best-time-to-see-northern-lights). If you still need tonight’s ranked list, use [where](/guides/where-to-see-northern-lights). If you still need the gates, use [how we decide](/methodology).

## Clothing, eyes, and cars

Do not quit because you are cold or blinded. Dress for the wait. Dim dash lights. Keep headlights off if you are safely parked. Do not stand in a traffic lane for a horizon glow. Give your eyes ten minutes after a phone screen.

A red headlamp is kinder than a white one. It still ruins a faint display if you point it north. Point it at your boots if you must.

## Mid-latitude versus oval posture

Under the oval, color can be overhead and obvious. At mid-latitudes it is usually a low green band on the north horizon. If you keep looking up, you will miss it. If you keep looking at the brightest thing in town, you will miss it.

Bring binoculars if you like; they are optional. A tripod is for photos, not for the yes/no. This site does not score ISO.

## Recap

How to see northern lights, recap: local card first, north second, darkness third, time fourth. Skip the trip on NO. Stay for the window on GO or MAYBE. Do not crowdsource a parking lot we never named.

## Checklist before you go out

1. Open the local page, not a national map.
2. Read status and the named obstacle.
3. If GO or MAYBE, check the window against −12° darkness.
4. Leave the brightest part of town if the card says glow.
5. Face north with a clear horizon.
6. Stay 30–60 minutes. Phone down except for a quick smear check.
7. Leave if the obstacle is “no oval reach.” Distance will not invent reach.

## What a phone smear is not

A green smudge on a long-exposure photo is not a second forecast, not a GO, and not a reason to drive another hour. It is optional evidence that some emission is there. Your eyes may still see nothing. That is normal on a MAYBE night.

We do not publish ISO, shutter, or white-balance recipes. Those belong on photography blogs. This page is about whether the sky is worth standing under.

## Safety

Ice, wildlife, rural roads, and cold are your problem, not the oval’s. Tell someone where you are going. Do not block a highway shoulder. Do not trespass. We will not argue with a landowner on your behalf.

Related: [Tonight](/) · [Near me](/near-me) · [Best time](/guides/best-time-to-see-northern-lights)

## Horizon versus overhead

If the card says overhead, you can look up. If it says horizon-only, look north along the lowest dark edge you can find. Trees, a south-facing valley, or a downtown wall will hide a horizon oval. Overhead color is harder to hide; glow and clouds can still hide it.

Binoculars help some people on a faint band. They are optional. A wide view with dark-adapted eyes is the default.

## After a MAYBE

Fix the named obstacle or stay in. Glow → leave the dome if you can. Mixed clouds → wait only if the deck is actually moving. Horizon-only → get a north edge, not a prettier south view. If you cannot fix it, treat MAYBE as a no for a special trip.

## After a GO

Still wait 30–60 minutes. Still face north. Still keep white light down. GO means the gates passed, not that a curtain is guaranteed in minute one. How to see northern lights on a GO night is still that posture, not a five-minute glance.
guides/methodology.md:
---
title: How We Decide If You Should Go Out
h1: How We Decide
---

Northern Lights Tonight is a local **go / maybe / no** for tonight. It is not a percentage, not a map tracker, and not affiliated with NOAA. This page is how we decide whether a night is worth a look at one place.

A local tonight reading is not a national Kp graphic. Magnetic latitude, live oval reach, darkness, clouds, and skyglow are evaluated for the headline point on the place page; Kp is context, not a nationwide yes or no.

## How we decide, in gate order

For each 30-minute slot that is dark enough (sun at or below **−12°**):

1. If aurora data is missing, we do not guess (**UNKNOWN**).
2. If the oval does not reach you, that slot is **NO**.
3. If clouds are socked in, **NO**.
4. Horizon-only plus city glow, or a bright moon on a horizon oval, cannot be **GO**.
5. Only a clear-enough sky with real reach can be **GO**. Otherwise **MAYBE**.

Slots that are still twilight are skipped (`not dark yet`) and do not vote. If the whole night never gets dark enough, the night is **NO** (summer high latitude). We do **not** average a weighted score. We do **not** print 73%.

## How to use a forecast card

Read the status, viewing window, and named obstacle together. **GO** still needs a dark northern view. **MAYBE** names an obstacle rather than a coin flip. **NO** means skip a special trip. **UNKNOWN** means current data is missing or stale, so we will not reuse an older color.

Quiet and mid-latitude places will show many NOs. That is the product working: a useful trip filter should reject nights when the oval, darkness, clouds, or skyglow do not line up.

If a window is open, give your eyes 30–60 minutes rather than testing the sky for five minutes from a porch. A phone camera may show a faint green smear before your eyes do, but that is a reason to keep looking, not a second forecast.

## Near window vs the rest of the night

The next ~90 minutes use NOAA SWPC **OVATION** grids (at the point and north along the horizon). Later tonight uses the **3-hour Kp forecast** plus, on pages that have a dossier, that place’s typical Kp bands. Mid-latitude and sub-oval pages cannot GO on that far window. A `/view` pin with no dossier cannot GO on the far window either.

The next hour is therefore stricter about the live oval, and more conservative about “later tonight.” A MAYBE in the far window is not a promise the oval will arrive.

## State pages use one headline point

A state is not the max of its cities. Colorado’s headline is the Fort Collins area, not Denver. Oregon’s headline is Baker City, not Portland. Other points can be listed; they do not get their own indexed URL.

A state night is “headline point, then contrast,” not “any city in the state said maybe.” If you need a ZIP, use near me rather than assuming the headline speaks for you.

## What UNKNOWN is for

UNKNOWN is a product decision. Missing or stale aurora data is not last hour’s GO with a disclaimer. Refusing to guess is part of the method. If every Wave 1 row is UNKNOWN, the homepage card says readings are paused.

## Sources

- NOAA Space Weather Prediction Center public products (OVATION and Kp).
- Cloud-cover data adapted from [Open-Meteo](https://open-meteo.com/) under [CC BY 4.0](https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/) (low / mid / high).
- Local sun and moon from the coordinates in the place dossier.

The browser never calls NOAA. Pages read snapshot files. Stale snapshots display **UNKNOWN**, not last hour’s GO.

The method is open on this page so a GO is auditable: darkness, reach, clouds, then glow and moon. It is not a neural net, and it is not a vibe.

Related: [Tonight](/) · [How to see](/guides/how-to-see-northern-lights) · [Best time](/guides/best-time-to-see-northern-lights)

## Confidence on the card

Confidence is high / medium / low on the card. It is not a percent. Conflicting short-term and overnight signals, missing clouds, or a far-window Kp call all push confidence down. Low confidence still never becomes a fake GO.

## Moon and glow

Moon is a blocker when it washes a horizon-only oval. It is not a nationwide kill switch. City glow is a blocker when the oval is weak and low. An overhead storm can punch through modest skyglow. The card names the issue instead of mixing moon, glow, and clouds into one mystery score.

## What we refuse to build

We do not average slots into 73%. We do not let the sunlit hours vote. We do not let a `/view` pin without a dossier GO on the far window. We do not take the max of every city in a state. The method is intentionally conservative so a GO means the gates passed, not that a map looked pretty.

If this page and a social post disagree, this page is the product. The social post is not a data source. How we decide stays on this URL so the gates can be checked.

## Worked example of the gates

Suppose OVATION says the oval reaches the headline point, clouds are mixed, the sun is below −12°, and the moon is down. That can be MAYBE (clouds) or GO (clear-enough). If the same oval is horizon-only and the city is a light dome, it cannot be GO even if Kp looks large on Twitter.

Suppose OVATION is missing. The night is UNKNOWN, not last night’s leftover GO. Suppose the sun never reaches −12°. The night is NO for darkness, even if the oval is wild.

These examples are the method, not extra data sources.

## What the far window is for

The far window exists so you can see whether later hours are even in play. It is not a second GO button. Mid-latitude pages cannot GO there. Pins without a dossier cannot GO there. If you only have time in the far window, read that as “maybe later, not a promise.”

## Related

[Tonight](/) · [How to see](/guides/how-to-see-northern-lights) · [Colorado example](/forecast/colorado) · [Fairbanks example](/forecast/fairbanks)

## Why the gates are ordered that way

Darkness first because a bright sky cannot show a night-sky event. Reach second because clouds over an oval that never arrives are a wasted wait. Clouds third because a clear sky with no oval is still a no. Glow and moon last because they modulate a weak horizon oval more than they cancel an overhead storm.

How we decide follows that order every night so the main issue on the card matches the first gate that failed, not a blended vibe.

## Slots and voting

Each 30-minute slot that is dark enough can fail or pass. Twilight slots do not vote. The night label is not an average of slots. One GO slot can make the night worth trying if clouds and reach agree. A night of NO slots stays NO.

How we decide also refuses to let the far window overrule a near-window UNKNOWN. Missing live oval data is not “use Kp instead and hope.”

How we decide GO MAYBE nights still names the obstacle. How we decide the night label is the first failed gate, not a blend. How we decide UNKNOWN nights is missing or stale aurora data, not a coin flip. Keep those three sentences next to the card if a social post disagrees.

Far-window Kp is context. Near-window OVATION is the live oval. Mid-latitude pages never use the far window as a GO. Summer high latitude can be a darkness NO even when the oval is active.

Confidence on the card stays high, medium, or low. It is not a percent and it is not a second status. Low confidence plus a MAYBE still means an obstacle was named. Missing cloud data can drop confidence without turning a reach-NO into a maybe.

Sources stay NOAA SWPC for the oval and Kp, Open-Meteo for clouds, and the dossier coordinates for sun and moon. The browser does not call those APIs. Stale files display UNKNOWN. That is the whole stack.

Gates decide how we label nights. Clouds decide how we label nights. Darkness decide how we label nights. Same five words, three gates, so the card matches the first failure.

## Northern lights tonight in the US

Northern lights tonight is a local question. A planetary Kp index is not a yes for your county. This homepage lists the US places we cover: each row is a GO, MAYBE, or NO from the same NOAA oval and cloud snapshot. Search a city or ZIP if your place is missing, or open a state page if you already know the name.

Use the table as a trip filter, not as a firework schedule. Quiet nights will show many NOs. That is the product working. Mid-latitude states need a strong storm. Oval-under places still lose to clouds and twilight. We do not invent a nationwide showtime, and we do not print a fake 73% chance.

The card above is a labeled sample reading (Fairbanks, Alaska when data is live), not a national average. If your sky is in Colorado or Ohio, ignore that sample and open the matching row. A Front Range city is not the same night as Interior Alaska.

## How to read the table

Each row is one covered place. Status is the night judgment. The named point under a state is the headline, not downtown by default. Colorado uses the Fort Collins area. Oregon uses Baker City, not Portland. If you live in the bright core, read the local page’s leave-the-city note before you treat a MAYBE as a porch event.

Rows can all be NO. Do not scroll looking for a hidden GO. If the oval is out of reach and clouds are socked in, we say no. UNKNOWN means we cannot judge right now because data is missing or stale. We would rather show UNKNOWN than last hour’s leftover GO.

Click a place to get hours, the main obstacle, and nearby states. The table is the index. The local page is the answer.

## What GO / MAYBE / NO means here

- **GO** — conditions line up well enough to try. Still look north, still need darkness, still wait.
- **MAYBE** — possible, with a named obstacle: horizon-only oval, mixed clouds, or city glow.
- **NO** — not worth a special trip tonight.
- **UNKNOWN** — cannot judge tonight. We will not guess.

This homepage never becomes a color map you have to decode. If you wanted a percentage, you will not find one. Methodology explains the gates in order: darkness, oval reach, clouds, then glow and moon.

## Location first, then the clock

There is no single US clock. Darkness arrives later in the west and later in summer. Alaska can stay too bright around the solstice even when the oval is active. A Lower 48 storm in May still needs a dark enough sky. Open the local page for the window; this homepage will not fake a 10:40 PM Eastern showtime.

If you asked “what time tonight,” the honest answer is: after it is actually dark at your coordinates, in the slots that are not socked in, while the oval still reaches you. That sentence only becomes a clock on a place page.

## Standing regions versus event nights

Alaska Interior, northern Minnesota, Michigan’s Upper Peninsula, and northern Maine sit closer to the oval. They are the usual US travel targets. They still have no-show nights. Colorado, Ohio, Illinois, Indiana, and similar mid-latitude states are event-only. Most nights are no. When they go, the useful sky is the dark north horizon away from the biggest light dome.

Seattle is often a cloud problem before it is a Kp problem. Chicago is almost never a downtown overhead curtain. Read the local FAQ instead of a viral phone photo from a darker county.

## What this site will not do

We do not list unverified parking lots. We do not sell tours. We are not affiliated with NOAA. Cloud data is adapted from Open-Meteo. The browser does not call NOAA; pages read snapshots. Stale snapshots display UNKNOWN.

If you need a ZIP, use near me. If you need season rather than this night, use best time. If you need posture — face north, wait, put the phone down — use how to see. If you need the gate order, use how we decide. The homepage job is the US table plus a search box.

## Using the search box

Type a US city, state, or 5-digit ZIP. We match it to a covered page or to a live pin that is not a second indexed URL. GPS is optional and runs only after you click Use my location. We do not store that point as an account. Southern-hemisphere coordinates get an unavailable reading, not a fake aurora score.

## Why northern lights near me needs a place

Northern lights near me is not a national map pin that follows your phone in the background. Aurora reach, clouds, and darkness change in tens of miles. A Kp 6 night in Minnesota is not a Kp 6 night on the Chicago lakeshore. This page exists to turn a city, state, or ZIP into a local GO / MAYBE / NO.

Type the place. If we have a covered page, we send you there. If we only have a coordinate match, we send you to a live reading that is not a second indexed URL. The search should land on one answer, not on a gallery of cities you will not drive to tonight.

## City, ZIP, or GPS

- **City or state** — best when you already know the name. “Fairbanks” and “Alaska” are different pages on purpose.
- **5-digit ZIP** — useful when the city name is ambiguous. We match US ZIPs in our list; we do not geocode the whole planet.
- **Use my location** — the browser asks once. We do not store that point in an account, cookie, or remarketing pixel. If you deny permission, type a city instead.

The form never requires an account. If GPS fails, the search box still works. If you are in the southern hemisphere, we will not invent a northern-hemisphere score.

## What happens after you search

A covered-place match opens the indexed local page: hours, main obstacle, nearby places, and the local FAQ. That is the page to bookmark. This page is only the search.

A live pin is for coordinates we do not give a dedicated URL. It is a reading, not a travel guide, and it stays noindex so it cannot cannibalize the city and state pages. Do not copy a pin URL into a blog as if it were the Fairbanks page.

If nothing matches, try the state name or a nearby larger city. We do not autocomplete every hamlet we cover.

## Why a national “near me” widget would lie

Oval grids are local. Cloud decks are local. Civil twilight is local. Moon and skyglow are local. A widget that returned one color for the entire Lower 48 would be entertainment, not a forecast. We would rather ask for a ZIP than pretend.

Marine cloud in Seattle, Front Range glow in Denver, and midnight sun in Fairbanks are different failure modes. The search box exists so those modes are not averaged.

## How to use the result

Once you land on a local page, read the status first, then the window, then the main issue. If the issue is city glow, leaving town may help. If the issue is clouds, a darker but still socked-in hill does not help. If the issue is no oval reach, driving twenty minutes does not change magnetic latitude enough.

This page is not a parking-lot finder. We will not list unofficial pullouts. Face north, wait 30–60 minutes if the window is open, and treat a phone smear as a hint, not a second forecast.

## Privacy on this page

Location is used to pick a place, then discarded from the product. Analytics, if enabled, records a path without query strings. You can opt out on the privacy policy page. NOAA and Open-Meteo are not called from your browser.

The tool should feel like a flashlight, not like a tracker. If that ever changes, the privacy policy will say so in plain language.

## Common mismatches

- **Wrong state** — Ohio is not Michigan. The oval and the lakeshore are different. Search again.
- **City vs state** — Fairbanks is not Alaska. Chicago is not Illinois. Both pairs exist so the language people type has a page.
- **Downtown vs headline** — Colorado’s headline is not Denver. If you meant “from my apartment,” read the glow note before you treat a MAYBE as a balcony event.
- **Photo from elsewhere** — a curtain in another time zone is not your ZIP.

The search should reduce those mismatches, not add a map for its own sake. If we add more states later, this search box is how you will reach them. Until then, the honest answer for an unmatched place is a live pin or a nearby covered page, never a fabricated GO.

If you came here from a national Kp graphic, type the ZIP anyway. Northern lights near me is the step that graphic skipped.

## What the matcher will not do

It will not invent a dedicated page for a hamlet we do not cover. It will not send you to a random overseas city. It will not keep GPS running in the background. It will not store the point in an account. If the query is empty, it asks you to type something. If the query is junk, it says no match.

## After you land

Bookmark the indexed local page, not this search page, if you come back often. Read status, window, obstacle. Use nearby links if you actually might drive that far. Ignore nearby links if they are other time zones you will not visit tonight.

## Examples of good queries

- `Fairbanks` → the Interior city page, not statewide Alaska.
- `Alaska` → statewide season and region, with a tonight card whose headline is the Interior.
- `80202` → a Colorado ZIP if it is in our list; otherwise try Denver or Colorado.
- `Chicago` → the city page, not Illinois.
- `Illinois` → the state page whose headline is not downtown Chicago.

Bad queries: empty string, a country name, a southern-hemisphere city you hope we will score anyway, or a street address. The matcher wants a US city, state, or ZIP.

## What you should do after a miss

Try the state. Try a larger nearby city. Use the homepage table if you only needed a covered place. Do not keep sending GPS if you already denied permission; type instead.

If we add your state later, the same box will be the entry. Until then a live pin is the honest fallback, and it stays noindex.

## Why ZIP beats a national map

A ZIP picks a point. A national map averages a continent. Oval reach at that point, the cloud deck at that point, and whether the sun is below −12° at that point are the three facts a ZIP can unlock. A color for “the United States” unlocks none of them.

Northern lights near me is that ZIP (or city) step. Type it, land, then read the card. If the card is NO, believe the named obstacle before you drive. If it is UNKNOWN, wait for data rather than inventing a color.
